title: INSERT: Adding a Row Into a Table
description: Learn how to use the INSERT statement to add a new row to a table in SQL Server.

data.text: SQL Server INSERT: Adding a Row Into a Table

Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **INSERT: Adding a Row Into a Table**. Learn how to use the INSERT statement to add a new row to a table in SQL Server. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of INSERT: Adding a Row Into a Table and be confident in applying it to your projects.
INSERT Syntax

data.title: Basic INSERT Syntax
data.content: Inserts a new row into the specified table with values for the listed columns.

data.text: In this syntax:

items: Specify the name of the table you want to insert into, optionally with the schema name (e.g., production.products).
List the columns in which you want to insert data, enclosed in parentheses and separated by commas.

If a column is not listed, SQL Server will provide a value automatically: the next IDENTITY value, a default value, the current timestamp for timestamp columns, NULL for nullable columns, or a computed value for computed columns.
Provide a corresponding value for each column in the column list within the VALUES clause.

data.text: Basic INSERT Example
The following example creates a promotions table and inserts a single row into it.

data.title: Create Table and Insert a Row
data.content: Creates the promotions table and inserts one row with promotion details.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE sales.promotions (
    promotion_id INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY (1, 1),
    promotion_name VARCHAR (255) NOT NULL,
    discount NUMERIC (3, 2) DEFAULT 0,
    start_date DATE NOT NULL,
    expired_date DATE NOT NULL
);  

INSERT INTO sales.promotions (
    promotion_name,
    discount,
    start_date,
    expired_date
)
VALUES
    (
        '2018 Summer Promotion',
        0.15,
        '20180601',
        '20180901'
    );

data.text: The promotion_id column is an identity column, so SQL Server provides its value automatically. After a successful insert, SQL Server returns a message like (1 row affected).

data.alt: SQL Server INSERT example output showing the inserted row in the promotions table

data.text: Insert and Return Inserted Values
To capture the inserted values, use the OUTPUT clause. This is useful when you need the identity value or other generated data back.

data.title: INSERT with OUTPUT Clause
data.content: Inserts a row and returns the promotion_id of the inserted row.
data.code:
INSERT INTO sales.promotions (
    promotion_name,
    discount,
    start_date,
    expired_date
) OUTPUT inserted.promotion_id
VALUES
    (
        '2018 Fall Promotion',
        0.15,
        '20181001',
        '20181101'
    );

data.text: To return multiple columns, specify them in the OUTPUT clause:

data.title: INSERT with OUTPUT Multiple Columns
data.content: Returns the promotion_id, name, discount, and dates of the inserted row.
data.code:
INSERT INTO sales.promotions (
    promotion_name,
    discount,
    start_date,
    expired_date
) OUTPUT inserted.promotion_id,
 inserted.promotion_name,
 inserted.discount,
 inserted.start_date,
 inserted.expired_date
VALUES
    (
        '2018 Winter Promotion',
        0.2,
        '20181201',
        '20190101'
    );

data.alt: SQL Server INSERT OUTPUT example showing the returned promotion_id

data.text: Insert Explicit Values into the Identity Column
Typically, you do not specify a value for the identity column because SQL Server provides it automatically. However, in situations like data migration, you may need to insert an explicit value.

data.title: Important
data.text: By default, IDENTITY_INSERT is OFF. You must explicitly turn it ON before inserting explicit values into an identity column, and turn it OFF afterward.

data.title: INSERT with Explicit Identity Value
data.content: Turns on identity insert, inserts a row with an explicit promotion_id, then turns identity insert off.
data.code:
SET IDENTITY_INSERT sales.promotions ON;

INSERT INTO sales.promotions (
    promotion_id,
    promotion_name,
    discount,
    start_date,
    expired_date
)
VALUES
    (
        4,
        '2019 Spring Promotion',
        0.25,
        '20190201',
        '20190301'
    );

SET IDENTITY_INSERT sales.promotions OFF;

data.text: Key Takeaways

data.title: INSERT Key Points
points: Use INSERT INTO with a column list and VALUES clause to add a new row.
Omitted columns receive automatic values: IDENTITY, default, timestamp, NULL, or computed values.
Use the OUTPUT clause to return inserted values, especially identity values.
To insert explicit values into an identity column, set IDENTITY_INSERT ON first, then OFF after.

This example demonstrates a production-ready implementation of **INSERT: Adding a Row Into a Table**. Study the code carefully, paying attention to error handling, type safety, and best practices. Try running it yourself and experiment with variations to deepen your understanding.

data.title: Production-Ready Implementation: INSERT: Adding a Row Into a Table
data.content: Complete working example demonstrating best practices and common patterns.
data.code:
-- SQL Example with Best Practices
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    c.email,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders,
    SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spent,
    AVG(o.order_total) AS average_order
FROM 
    sales.customers c
LEFT JOIN 
    sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    AND o.order_date >= DATEADD(year, -1, GETDATE())
WHERE 
    c.is_active = 1
    AND c.created_date >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY 
    c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.email
HAVING 
    COUNT(o.order_id) > 0
ORDER BY 
    total_spent DESC
OPTION 
    (RECOMPILE);

-- Performance Tips:
-- 1. Use appropriate indexes on join columns
-- 2. Avoid SELECT * - specify only needed columns
-- 3. Filter early with WHERE clause
-- 4. Use JOINs instead of subqueries when possible
